briefing.lede: Anthropic wrote the memo everyone in agents pretends they read. Actually read it.
briefing.steal_this: Their rule of thumb: start with the simplest workflow, add agentic complexity only when the simpler thing measurably fails. Steal the discipline, not the architecture.
briefing.what_happened: Anthropic's engineering team published their field notes from a year of building agents with Claude: workflows versus agents, when to add complexity, and why the simplest thing that works usually wins. It is the closest thing the industry has to an operator's manual for agentic systems.
briefing.why_it_matters: Every agent startup pitch deck name-drops agentic workflows — this is the source text. It draws the line the whole market now argues about: augmented LLMs with structure beat autonomous agents with vibes. If you read one thing on this shelf, read this.

takeaways: Complexity is a budget — spend it where it pays
items.title: Building Effective Agents

briefing.lede: The paper that taught language models to think out loud, then do something about it.
briefing.steal_this: The loop is the primitive. Before reaching for a framework, prototype the ReAct loop by hand — you will learn more about your task in an afternoon than in a week of configuration.
briefing.what_happened: Yao et al. interleaved chain-of-thought reasoning with tool actions — reason, act, observe, repeat — and showed it beats pure reasoning or pure acting on knowledge-heavy and decision-heavy benchmarks. It reads obvious now. It was not obvious then.
briefing.why_it_matters: Every agent loop you have ever seen is a descendant of ReAct. The trajectory format — Thought, Action, Observation — became the instruction set of the agentic era. Knowing the original tells you exactly what the modern abstractions are hiding.

queries: react reasoning acting language models agents
takeaways: Reason plus act beats reason alone
Simple loops compose into complex systems

briefing.lede: The best free on-ramp to agents that is not a 40-hour video graveyard.
briefing.steal_this: Their progression — prompt, then tool, then loop, then system — is the fastest known path from zero to a working agent. Copy the ladder for onboarding anyone.
briefing.what_happened: Hugging Face shipped a hands-on course that walks from LLM basics through tool use, code agents, and multi-agent setups — with real exercises against real models, not slides about the future. It treats you like a builder, not an audience.
briefing.why_it_matters: Most AI courses teach you to watch. This one teaches you to ship, which is the only credential that counts for forward-deployed work. Finish the capstone and you walk away with a portfolio piece, not a certificate.

takeaways: Tool use is the first real skill
items.title: Hugging Face Agents Course

briefing.lede: Four design patterns that turn 'let's add agents' from a slogan into a spec.
briefing.steal_this: Reflection loops: have the agent critique its own output before a human ever sees it. The cheapest quality gain in the book.
briefing.what_happened: Andrew Ng's team distilled agentic work into four patterns — reflection, tool use, planning, multi-agent collaboration — taught through working AutoGen code. Short, dense, and mercifully free of hype.
briefing.why_it_matters: Patterns are portable across frameworks, which is the entire point: frameworks churn, patterns persist. In a client meeting, speaking in patterns is how you sound like the person who has done this before.

takeaways: Teach the ladder, not the tool

briefing.lede: OpenAI stopped selling the magic and started handing out the shovels.
briefing.steal_this: Guardrails as first-class primitives. Whatever framework you use, design your failure modes before your happy path.
briefing.what_happened: OpenAI open-sourced its Agents SDK — lightweight primitives for multi-agent orchestration: agents, handoffs, guardrails. No new model, no keynote theatrics. Just the plumbing their own teams use, handed to everyone.
briefing.why_it_matters: When the model labs open-source the orchestration layer, the message is clear: the models are converging, and the leverage is in the system around them. For builders, the primitives are now free — the differentiation is your workflow, your evals, your domain.

takeaways: Primitives are free; workflows are the moat
items.title: OpenAI's Agents SDK goes open source

briefing.lede: USB-C for AI tools: the standard that decides whether your agent talks to everything or nothing.
briefing.steal_this: Ship your internal tools as MCP servers once, and every agent your team builds can use them. One integration surface, infinite consumers.
briefing.what_happened: Anthropic open-sourced the Model Context Protocol — a standard way for models to discover and call tools, read files, and query databases. It turned integration from a consulting project into a config file, and the ecosystem exploded with thousands of MCP servers in months.
briefing.why_it_matters: Standards decide markets. If you do forward-deployed or solutions engineering, MCP is the difference between a bespoke integration and a reusable one — which is the difference between a project and a practice. Learn it before your clients ask.

briefing.lede: The newsletter senior engineers actually read — because it reads like a postmortem, not a pep talk.
briefing.steal_this: His working-in-public habit — writing down what you learned from every engagement. That notebook becomes your interview answers.
briefing.what_happened: Gergely Orosz's Pragmatic Engineer covers how software actually gets built inside real companies: leveling, system design, AI tooling adoption, and the unglamorous mechanics of shipping. It is the trade press for people who do the work.
briefing.why_it_matters: Forward-deployed and solutions roles are judged on judgment, not just code. Reading how senior engineers think about trade-offs is the cheapest way to borrow a decade of scar tissue.

briefing.lede: The clearest writer on what breaks when LLM prototypes meet production — and how to fix it.
briefing.steal_this: Evaluation-driven development: write the eval before the feature. Steal it for every client engagement.
briefing.what_happened: Chip Huyen writes long, evidence-heavy essays on LLM engineering: evals, RAG failure modes, agent reliability. Her book AI Engineering became the field's operating manual. The blog is the free version of the same rigor.
briefing.why_it_matters: Anyone can ship a toy agent. Forward-deployed engineers get hired to make it survive contact with users. This is the curriculum for that second, harder skill — and being fluent in it is how you signal you know where the bodies are buried.

takeaways: Toy agents are easy; production is the job
Know where the bodies are buried
